I think this is still the common individual goal in American culture, but it has been severely disrupted as the 'conventional' means to it have become increasingly inviable. Also, we have become a predominantly urban society. Most of us now live in cities where property ownership is largely impossible for all but a very tiny, shrinking, minority. The so-called American dream is in decline because the middle-class contract it was based on has been broken by finance and business cultures that have become dysfunctional. What is now often referred to as 'late-stage Capitalism' as to suggest that it has entered its cannibalistic end-game.

But people are thinking about home ownership in new and unconventional ways as the infrastructure that a middle-class standard of living depended on is no longer as critical and the nature of work and housing themselves are changing. Where you live matters decreasingly to how you live. Much of that has to do with the rise of the Internet and information technology. However, it is now expanding to industrial independence --to an emerging potential for production at/near home. And with that comes a rediscovered capability to house oneself. The new dream home is now as often a collection of repurposed shipping containers or a cob cottage made by hand on the edge of wilderness as it is a cabin on a lake or a McMansion in the suburbs.

So now you have a lot of young people aspiring not to a mortgage on a house in Levittown but a mortgage-free Tiny House on the edge of wilderness built with their own hands, potentially in a cohousing or intentional community context. They are not aspiring to become a VP in a corporation but to own their own business on the Internet and supplement that with what they can produce for themselves. Intentional communities and cohousing are now more popular than ever as young people turn to the idea of community interdependence as a solution to the destruction of the middle-class contract. So many aren't aspiring to home ownership as much as to participation in creating new coherent communities where they can leverage the power of the group on affordability of what they need. Everything is cheaper in volume. Everything is cheaper when shared.

Some now aspire to a 'digital nomad' lifestyle where one trades ownership of a lot of physical property for a life wandering the world. There are now luxury 'coliving' services where, for a flat fee per month, you can live in any of a growing global network of group home facilities akin to small intimate hotels with companion 'coworking' facilities designed for online business. So you can just follow the seasons or the global migration of popular 'start-up culture' centers.

In the Maker community there is an undercurrent idea called 'unplugging'; where the emerging and cheapening tools of independent production are leveraged on a progressive discount on the cost of living by whittling away personal dependency on the market. We may still be a long way from being able to make our own smartphones and computers from scratch, but just about everything else is something you can, in some way, make for yourself with a steadily dropping bar of skill level. There really is no technical reason a person today cannot, by themselves, build their own home --and up to 80% of the cost of a conventional home in the US is labor cost, with most of that spent on interior finishing. (because we have long designed homes not for people but for banks whose chief concern is maximizing their expense to optimize their 'value') There's no good reason why an adequate, comfortable, home isn't as easy as a piece of Ikea furniture.

Some people see unplugging as the new strategy for early retirement. Instead of accumulating conventional wealth to achieve some personal economic escape velocity (ie. having enough stored wealth that one can live on the automatic interest it produces), we save for a set of tools that let us make a home and turn it into a personal engine of subsistence, and then unplug from the market economy as a community cultivating and sharing its own production knowledge.

The American dream is definitely not what it was, but it need not be dead. The core problem is the increasing, fundamental, inhumanity of the people we once entrusted with the custodianship of that dream. So, we take it back.

I look at it this way, it can be a smart financial move. My total housing costs (mortgage, taxes, not-minimums insurance) are less than $500/month for a historic 1930's built brick tudor (visually pleasing architectural style that has value outside of money for me). This is a 2,200 sq/ft house on an acre of land.

To put that into perspective, the cheapest, shittiest 1-bed apartments (all Section 8) around here go for about $600/month without any kind of utilities much less insurance. It is $100 cheaper per month for me to own a home, though I bet my utilities costs eat up that difference... but my Quality of housing for the price is so far beyond what else is out there for the money that it's not even funny.

And that's not even taking into consideration what happens when you sell. This is my 4th house, I've sold 3 others and my WORST CASE was walking away having paid roughly $100/month to live in the home (and update it, have insurance, etc...) Best case, I was paid quite significantly to have owned the property, enough that we paid off my wifes remaining school loans AND still had cash for a 20% down payment on the next house. Make no mistake, owning a home is without question a LIABILITY, you absolutely have to pay the bank their money each and every month, come hell or high water. You are 100% on the hook for any damages that occur, anything that breaks or needs service and that all takes money. And counting on housing prices to go up is 100% speculation (and has bitten many an ignorant person in their ass). You can dig a deep financial hole by trying to float too big of a loan, this is reflected in terms like "House poor", "Upside down" and "Underwater" ~ I have an in-law who is just BARELY keeping himself afloat with his house loan payments and I honestly don't think they will make it through a 2nd year of ownership without getting behind. I'm guessing that his payment is close to $1300/month, and I know he's paying $1200/month in child care and they have 2 new vehicle payments (I'll bet $800/moth is safe to assume on those). Money is so tight for them that over Christmas, they gave out a bag of M&M's to each family as gifts... not each family member (2~3 per family).

As for younger americans, I think the push to herd into urban centers is strong. There's near zero chance of owning something in those places, you have to go to the 'Burbs and there's a social stigma against that until married with kids. None of my young cousins (20~30, 8 in total) want to live outside of an urban area. Now, I'm From rural, Wyoming, and I did urban from 22~30 myself with no thoughts of owning a home at that time. It's been a breath of fresh air since getting back to a rural environment. I suspect that the divide between home ownership and renting will Also be the divide between urban living and rural, with a few who opt for suburbs.
